title: Value Investing Isn't Holding Long — It's Stashing a Big Pile in the Bank First
dek: No value investor ever went from broke to rich doing value investing; they made money first, then chose to live the value-investing life. Buffett's real engine is 60 to 70 wholly owned subsidiaries pumping cash, not a compounding myth.
why: This episode is dense with information, but the guest's judgments are quite absolute, and the host explicitly says at the end that he partly disagrees. Suited to anyone who wants a complete, counterintuitive teardown.
who: Investors who already believe in value investing but haven't thought through where the principal and the cash flow come from, and founders who want to understand Buffett's actual wealth structure.
skip: The host's closing monologue after about 1:43 is optional; the guest portion before it is denser.

points.h: The story of the two old ladies in heaven is something we made up
points.body: In 1999, new apartments along Beijing's Third and Fourth Ring Roads sold for 4,000 yuan a square meter and wouldn't move; downtown single-story houses were only a few hundred yuan a square meter, and people were unwilling to borrow from banks because they felt debt was shameful. Fang Yan was working at an ad agency at the time, and to convince the market he first had to convince the people around him, so in the office he made up the story of the Chinese old lady who saved her whole life to buy a house and the American old lady who took out a loan, bought a house, and paid it off before she died, then spread it through the media. Once he believed it himself, he bought his first place in 2000, set a rule of buying one a year, and planned to retire at 40. The detail shows: many wealth beliefs treated as common sense trace back to a single piece of marketing.

points.h: Companies that sell advice can't go public
points.body: Fang Yan ran an ad agency early on, and his clients went public one after another. He asked a securities firm whether they could take him public too, and the answer was: your kind of company is a ‘people-based company’ — you sell ideas, and to come up with more ideas you have to hire more people; only a ‘capital-based company’ that pools capital together generates enormous force, and only that is fit to go public. Restaurants are the least fit to list, because one location being good doesn't mean a hundred will be; Haidilao could list because it first built a condiment factory, a standardized product. That classification directly decided his later move to give up the billionaire dream and buy stocks instead — ‘once you buy a stock, you are the listed company.’

points.h: Munger said value investing is a big pile of money in the bank
points.body: At the Daily Journal shareholders meeting someone asked what value investing is, and Munger's answer wasn't the textbook line: keep a big pile of money in the bank, then patiently wait for an opportunity. Fang Yan thinks this is the truth — no value investor ever went from broke to rich doing value investing; they made money first, then chose to live the value-investing life. India's Pabrai also sold his company, put a big pile in the bank, and waited for opportunities. The companion rule is ‘if you want to be a value investor, you have to live the value-investing life’: Buffett keeps three to four hundred billion US dollars in cash in the bank, and has lived for over fifty years in a $30,000 house in a fourth-tier city.

points.h: Buffett's engine is 60 to 70 subsidiaries, not compounding
points.body: Fang Yan breaks it down: over fifty years of doing business, Buffett gained control of 60 to 70 wholly owned subsidiaries, and those subsidiaries in turn control several hundred grandchild companies. The CEOs' job is to endlessly generate free cash flow, but they have no right to deploy it; the cash flows up to Berkshire and a few big heads allocate it. The insurance group contributes only about a quarter of revenue; more comes from companies making gloves, old work boots, T-shirts, hats, bricks, wedding rings, DQ ice cream, See's Candies — the eating, drinking, and daily life of ordinary people. These businesses don't need outstanding CEOs; almost anyone can follow the rules. So Buffett isn't 100% trading stocks — he controls a large real-economy conglomerate in America.

points.h: If you've never run a company, you can't understand one
points.body: Duan Yongping said ‘you'd best run a company,’ and Fang Yan says that line stings as much as Munger's: if you don't build a company yourself, don't hire people, don't negotiate with clients, don't get hurt by clients, you don't know how complex the business world is. His experience as a boss is that ‘there is no company that doesn't lose money’ — embezzlement, employee negligence, fake invoices for reimbursement, all unavoidable. That's why he won't invest in restaurants. He also cites a brand caught in a scandal: it claimed 6 billion a year, with 300 million in profit on a single-brand basis, yet the group was losing money — essentially it was selling vegetables for others for free, and the money was earned by the vegetable and soy sauce sellers and the mall landlords.

points.h: The 80/20 rule understates it — it's 2% winning and 98% losing
points.body: Fang Yan thinks that over a long horizon it isn't 20% winning and 80% losing, but 2% of people making money and 98% being losers. His own experience: in March 2015 he pulled his money out of the GF Securities branch at SOHO on the East Third Ring Road, and the manager walked him out and said only two people at their branch had made big money. What he withdrew was 120 million, on principal of a bit over 13 million. Three months later the whole market collapsed and no one could get out. He forced his nephew to get out too; the nephew couldn't resist and went back in, and he had to force him out again.

points.h: Tie yourself to the mast or you won't hold on to the money
points.body: After pulling out the 120 million the market kept rising, with daily gains that could reach over 10 million, and Fang Yan himself was struggling. His method was to go to ICBC and buy a product he couldn't withdraw — a bond issued by ICBC, benchmarked to foreign exchange, with a six-month contract, paying 10,000 yuan a day, but absolutely not withdrawable. He says there's only one way to tie yourself down, and that's a physical method, like Odysseus tying himself to the mast and having his crew seal their ears with wax. The day the market collapsed, June 15, happened to be his wife's birthday; the whole restaurant was sighing and panicking, and only their table was happy and relaxed.

points.h: Buying a jet, chasing celebrities, climbing Everest are reverse indicators
points.body: Fang Yan says this isn't a curse, it's objective reality: no one has climbed Everest and then had their business thrive afterward. Climbing Everest is a show-off mentality; getting up isn't that hard, you rely on a Sherpa team to help you, and with two-plus months of back-and-forth training the cost is enormous. Zhang Chaoyang himself reflected on it, saying that for Everest he spent several months not at the company, and that was the one thing he most shouldn't have done. Away from the company year-round, with employees watching you climb Everest on TV every day, the team's mindset changes. Private jets are the same: in America they're bought by 20 or 30 people crowdfunding, and with vast, sparsely populated land and inconvenient transport there's an objective need; China has no such need, and this game pulled off one con in China, and now fewer and fewer people buy them.

quotes.text: So we made up that famous story — the two old ladies meeting in heaven — that was made up, that was made up by us.
No value investor ever went from broke to a tycoon doing value investing — none. Every value investor made money first, then chose to live the value-investing life.

If you don't build a company yourself, don't hire people, don't negotiate with clients, don't get hurt by clients, you don't know how complex the business world is, and you can't understand a company.
There's only one way to tie yourself down — you have to think of a physical way to tie yourself down.
The most terrifying thing is always this: you take three steps forward and one step back — that's hesitation. The most terrifying thing is indecision, and then half-believing, half-doubting.
